The final season of The Boys is, without exaggeration, one of the most frustrating collapses I’ve seen from a once-promising show. What started as a sharp, cynical, violent satire ended in something that feels rushed, directionless, and strangely empty. The finale itself barely qualifies as a finale. It plays more like a troll attempt at “subverting expectations” than an actual conclusion with emotional or narrative payoff. Nothing lands. Not emotionally, not visually, not thematically. The death of Frenchie is probably the clearest example of how badly this season handles its own writing. A character death can work when it reshapes the emotional state of the story or meaningfully impacts the surviving cast. Here, it happens so late and so abruptly that it has essentially no weight. The show treats it like a major dramatic moment, but there’s no time left for consequences, grief, or reflection. It’s shock value without substance. And the action — unbelievably bad. Especially in an era where franchises like John Wick completely redefined modern fight choreography. There is no excuse anymore for action scenes this sloppy, weightless, and incoherent. The fights in this season feel edited to hide limitations rather than showcase skill or tension. Nothing feels dangerous. Nothing feels memorable. Characters with godlike powers somehow manage to make every confrontation look dull. What’s worse is that the writing no longer has the intelligence or sharpness to compensate for the weak spectacle. Character arcs collapse into nonsense. Motivations change depending on what the script needs in the moment. Emotional beats are rushed through at hyperspeed, while pointless scenes drag endlessly. Several conclusions feel less like deliberate endings and more like the writers simply ran out of ideas and decided to stop. The bitter part is that you can still see traces of what the show used to be. That’s what makes the disappointment worse. This wasn’t some generic bad series from the beginning. It had style, energy, satire, and momentum. Watching it decay into this bloated, cynical mess leaves an incredibly sour aftertaste. By the end, the entire season feels like a waste of time. The only genuinely positive thought left is hoping the cast got paid extremely well, because this is not the kind of material anyone should proudly put forward as the culmination of their work.

It botched both the Finale and the final season. That doesn't mean the beats weren't there. It means its way of getting to those beats was awful. -- Ryan ending up with MM: That should have been their plotline this season. MM kind of wandered around with nothing to do, and they literally hid Ryan for the majority of the season. But what if, after Ryan gets beaten up and Butcher is a prick to him, MM takes him under his wing? What might have been the most interesting choice in the finale had no buildup or lead into the decision. -- Butcher's death should have been after the Piano Man montage: What gives UE more to fight for? Having a child. What makes his argument more compelling? Having the life Butcher was never able to have. THAT should have been the final moments, an apathetic Butcher who has nothing left in life, while everyone else has moved on, essentially becoming a domestic terrorist, waiting to be put out of his misery by someone. It would also have earned UE by killing him. -- The same way The Deep was killed by his own people, Homelander should have been killed by normal people. In this scenario, Homelander actually enacts his partial genocide, mowing down innocents. All of the blast stuff still works, but Butcher and The Boys let him walk away, having to live as a normal person. But it isn't too long before he is encountered by his most faithful followers and ripped limb to limb. -- Soldier Boy should have just gone to Mexico to do blow and bang hookers after his disappointment in trying to change Homelander. Obviously, the Cara Vought thing was massively dumb. But what would have been more interesting is if Soldier Boy actually showed a modicum of change, realizing he was going to have to go back in the box if he couldn't pretend to be paternal. But in seeing all of his "Vought Rising" peeps (which should have been the one ep with Bombshell), he decides he can actually be a hero and change Homelander. But as Homelander continues to grow out of control, he leaves him, like a 50s dad would to go get cigarettes. -- The virus needed to be tossed aside after the second episode in order for the Frenchie/Radiation plotline to work and breathe appropriately. And if Kamiko WAS that harshly radiated, it might have been more interesting if Frenchie's insistence on being close to her killed him instead, making Kamiko's dive back into silence and grief a little more understandable. The whole season felt rushed and unfocused. These would be the changes I would have made to bring it back to its first 2 seasons' quality.

I study cognitive science/philosophy, and in fact, I think my undergraduate thesis may be on the neurological basis for meta-rationalism(what is/are the relationship(s) between mental complexes that gives us metacognition, and what about the complexes and stimuli we don't meta-cognate?)  and if you understand what that means, then you also know why I find this character so interesting. She's basically a Meta-rational agent suffering from metabolically induced unbounded rationality. She suffers from her own capacity for intellectual consideration and search. While its not a bad show (i'm mostly leaning into the criticism for the fun of it) i just have to point out the extreme irony baked into the entire thing. The sappiness of a lot of super hero movies, the quippy one liners, the endless milking of franchises, the critique of celebrity worship in a show about an evil mega corporation that is made by AMAZON, which ends with a billion spin offs, one of which stars one of its most heinous characters as the lead, where half of the lines end up swearing or mentioning dick. The boys is definitely an example of how a show can become the very thing it wants to criticise if it goes on too long or the writing changes. Maybe that makes it work of genius. Idk. I can't overlook the positives of the show with that being said. The characters and premise are phenomenal. Those earlier episodes had such amazing momentum and tension that kept me hooked week to week. I feel like on the whole it did an amazing job of building its world and exploring its premise and those in-universe commercials/shows/bits alone made every season a treat to watch. It's very unlikely we'll ever get a show like this again that isn't just an extension of this franchise which is kind of sad. But its been a fun ride and i have to give props to Kripke and the showrunners for bringing this world to life and giving us one of TV's best villains in recent memory. It will be really interesting to see how this show is remembered over time. I'm honestly gonna miss it.

This article is my impression after watching the finale of *The Boys*. I originally wrote it in Chinese and used AI to translate it into English. Homelander’s begging lines in the end were truly character-destroying! In my opinion, Homelander’s character revolves around two core keywords: **A profound lack of love** combined with an extreme craving for it — including (a) the love of family/parents, and (b) the love and adoration of others. **Extreme arrogance** and the pursuit of supreme power, while unknowingly using all the wrong methods to achieve it. **Keyword 1: The Search for Love** At his core, Homelander is someone starved of love. From the very beginning, his uncontrollable urge to drink breast milk whenever he sees it is a clear symbol of his desperate “pursuit of maternal love.” Later, his fight for custody of his son Ryan (constantly trying to build a father-son relationship) and his attention toward Soldier Boy (searching for paternal love) all reflect his attempt to compensate for the severe absence of normal family affection in his childhood. At the same time, he constantly seeks the love of others. Yet because of his volatile temper, brutality, and zero tolerance for betrayal, he feels everyone around him leaving him one by one. His final desire to become a literal god is also, in essence, a wish for the whole world to love him the way people love Christ. He is still searching for love. The paradox is that the more desperately he seeks others’ love, the less he can tolerate disloyalty, and the more he pushes everyone away. Ryan’s behavior in the series was also poorly written. At the beginning, it was somewhat reasonable — caught between Butcher and Homelander, he was understandably hesitant. But as the story progressed, it became clear that Butcher only saw Ryan as a tool to use against Homelander. In contrast, Homelander consistently showed genuine parental affection toward Ryan and tried to bring him back to his side. Even after Ryan betrayed him multiple times, and despite Homelander’s extreme hatred of betrayal, he never went for the kill (he ultimately spared Ryan’s life). Yet in the end, Ryan helped Butcher kill his own biological father. While Homelander’s death may fit the plot, from a family perspective, Ryan’s character is truly despicable. You can leave a father you don’t like. You can even choose not to be present when someone else kills him. But to actively show up and help murder your own father? Is that something a son with normal human emotions would do? **Keyword 2: The Pursuit of Power** Homelander’s lust for power is both the cause and consequence of his search for love. Seeking love is the goal; acquiring power is the means. The entire *The Boys* series, from Season 1 to the final season, is essentially the story of Homelander’s “gradual rise to power.” Through this process, his personality — arrogant, narcissistic, volatile, and deeply oppressive — is vividly portrayed. Up until the moments before his death, this characterization was very successful. However, I strongly suspect the writers either changed or lost the plot, because they gave Homelander an extremely pathetic, groveling begging monologue right before his death. It completely turned him into a ridiculous clown. But Homelander is **not** a clown! You can call him emotionally defective, a man-child, a dictator, or a Nazi — but he is absolutely not a clown character. In my view, his death should have been more like how Hitler saw himself and how he chose to die — that would have been true to the character. If Homelander had said something like “You finally have the chance to kill me” to Butcher and then fought to the death, instead of begging pathetically, it would have been consistent with his established personality. Homelander despises weakness and groveling — this is clearly shown in his attitude toward The Deep and in the humiliating lines he delivers to him at the end. He hates that kind of person the most, so he would never, even in death, utter the kind of dialogue the writers forced on him. As a result, Homelander’s character was ruined and the series ended on a sour note. The same goes for the sloppy deaths of other characters in the finale. The character I used to really like, **Ashley**, suffered the same fate. She had a very well-developed arc in previous seasons — her internal conflict about leaving, her greed for status, and her gradual descent into desperation. Her transformation at the end of Season 4 should have marked a true awakening, yet in the first few episodes of Season 5 she went back to hedonistic indulgence and clinging to illusory power (obsessing over the vice presidency). Only in the very last episode did she suddenly decide to flee and help the protagonists. This shift didn’t feel like a genuine character development for Ashley — it felt like the writers needed to wrap up the show and forcibly wrote her off. It completely destroyed the perfect character arc she had built up before. The production team may indeed have run out of budget for big scenes, but they didn’t have to ruin the best characters in *The Boys* — Homelander and Ashley. What a shame. --- (本文是我对黑袍纠察队最后一集的观感, 我是用中文写的, 我用AI来翻译成了英文: 因为我还没有权限单独发帖, 只能回复, 我就发在这里.) 最后祖国人的求饶台词,真的是毁人设! 我认为, 祖国人角色的关键词就是两个: 1.缺爱,又极其渴望地想获得爱, 包括 ①寻找家庭亲人之爱, ② 获得他人之爱. 2.极其自傲, 寻求无上的权力, 但却不自知的使用着错误的方法. 关键词1: 寻爱 祖国人本质上是个缺爱的人. 从最早的喝母乳, 一看到母乳就忍不住想喝, 是"追寻母爱"的象征. 后来争夺儿子(一直试图建立起亲子关系), 关注同士兵男孩(寻找父爱), 都体现出祖国人在试图弥补"童年正常家庭情感关系"的严重缺失. 同时, 他又一直想获得他人之爱, 但由于他的喜怒无常, 暴虐, 不能容忍背叛, 导致他感到所有人都在一个个的离他而去. 祖国人最后想成为真神, 也是希望世上所有人都能像爱基督一样来爱他. 依然在寻找爱. 悖论是, 他越是寻求他人之爱, 也就越不能容忍不忠, 也就越是推开了所有人. 祖国人的儿子 Ryan 的行为, 在这部剧里被编写的也很失败. 一开始还算正常, 他被布切尔和祖国人两边争取, 他犹豫不决. 但后来观众就能发现, 布切尔只是把 Ryan 当作工具人, 以对付祖国人. 但祖国人从头到尾都一直对Ryan 保有亲情感, 想拉回他到自己身边的, 即使Ryan 几次背叛祖国人, 即使如此, 在最狠的时候祖国人也没对他下死手(要知道祖国人是极其痛恨背叛的, 但他最终还是留下了Ryan 的命). 但Ryan 最后却帮着布切尔把亲爹给干掉了, 虽然祖国人的死符合剧情发展, 但从家庭关系来说, Ryan这个人的人品, 就真的是令人不耻. 你可以离开你不喜欢的老爸, 你可以在布切尔干你老爸时不在场, 但你却到现场帮着杀你的老爸, 这是正常情感的儿子能干的事吗? 关键2: 获取权力 祖国人的获取权力欲望, 是和他的"寻爱"互为因果的. 寻爱是目的, 获得权力是手段. 整个黑袍剧集, 从第一季到最后一季, 都是祖国人"一步步获取权力"的过程, 并且从中体现出祖国人的性格 -- 自傲, 自负, 喜怒无常, 极具压迫感. 可以说, 在他死前, 这些塑造都是很成功的. 但我很怀疑编剧是换人了还是怎么想的, 居然给祖国人设计了死前说出了极其毁人设的低三下四的求饶台词. 这让祖国人就彻底变成了一个可笑的小丑. 但祖国人可不是小丑! 他的性格, 情感追求, 权力追求, 你可以说他有情感缺陷, 巨婴, 或独裁纳粹, 但他完全不是小丑人设! 我认为他的死, 要更像希特勒对自己的看法和死法, 才是符合人设的. 如果祖国人最后对布切尔说"你现在终于有机会杀死我了", 然后奋战而死, 而不是低下的求饶, 才是前后一致的人设. 祖国人是最讨厌低三下四的人了, 这在他对深海的态度, 和最后羞辱深海的台词中, 已经鲜明的体现出了这一点. 他最讨厌那种人, 所以祖国人至死也不会说出编剧现在给他的那种台词的. 所以, 祖国人的人设被毁了, 烂尾了. 就像最后一集中其他的人草草死法一样. 我之前非常喜欢的ashley也一样, 她在之前有一个很好的人物地位变化和情感变化塑造, 她对离去的纠结, 她对地位的贪恋, 她一步步步入绝境. 在第四季的最后一集中, 她的变异, 本应使她已经觉醒了, 但编剧却让她在第五季的前几集还是醉生梦死的放纵, 还是在贪权(迷恋虚幻的副总统地位), 直到最后一集才突然想要逃离,才帮了主角团一把.  这种转变令人感觉不像是ashley的真正转变, 而是编剧必须要结束全剧了, 硬生生的让她下线的. 真的是毁掉了ashley之前的完美弧光. 剧组的确是没钱拍大场面, 但你不能把黑袍中最棒的角色的人设也都毁掉呀 -- 祖国人, ashley 真的是太可惜了.

It started to become apparent during season 4 that the showrunners had little real idea what to do with Ryan, and him constantly flipping between sides started to feel frustrating. Now that the series is done, it's extremely frustrating, though sadly not surprising to see that Ryan ultimately didn't matter much. Okay. The finale was rushed and that made is so much worse. BUUUUUUUUUUUT! I still think it was satisfactory. Although Homelander didn't really snap, i think the "i am going to kill all unbelievers" line when going off script was terrifying. Like imagine living in that universe and the one man who you see as immortal says he's going to kill everyone, not funny stuff. Most of the stuff expected to be seen WAS in fact seen. Starlight got her revenge, so did Butcher. I loved the crowbar reference to the comic and Ryan was great substitute for the comic Black Noir. People complain about powerscalling and i kinda agree, but you also have to take into consideration the fact, that the final fight was a 3v1 and Homelander doesn't really have any actual fighting experience. Ryan is also literally Homelander's equivalent with all his powers, although weaker since 1. He's a teen and 2. Homelander had V1. But that was easily fixed with the addition on Butcher, who literally has powers due to the tentacle cancer and Kimiko, who probably got even more powerful after the radiation experiment. Overall, i'd say the fight was fair. It wasn't like he died after 2 minutes, Homelander held his ground for fairly long. He didn't even lose the fight, we was depowered. The scene was a nice paralel with S3 when he was first held down by Butcher and HUGHIE (If damn Hughie could hold down Homelander, i'm sure his own son could do it too, despite him having V1). Emotions were managed appropriately. Homelanders send off was satisfying, with him being humiliated in front of the whole world and ultimately killed by Butcher, which again perfectly mirrored the comics. Kimiko seeing Frenchie was more emotional than his death and served as a nice conclusion to their storyline, with her giving up all the hatred and instead choosing love. Terror dying as a symbol for Butchers last bit of humanity perishing was amazing, with Ryan also telling him he's not a good person, just as him going to Vought to release the virus. Ultimately for it to come down as Hughie vs Butcher, magnificent. Butcher realising his true intents and seeing his brother in Hughie, before dying, though choosing not to release the virus. Yes, there were things that i'm VERY VERY VERY disappointed with, as i mentioned, the episode felt rushed. I also wish we saw more of the impact after Homelander died. Also, the whole White House plan was stupid and in reality, the boys would DEFINETLY lose. V1 should have given Homelander much more power. The ENTIRE season was treated rather like a setup for the Vought Rising series than a final season and the entire plot of what we saw in the finale should have been at least TWO episodes. I am though still content with all the conclusions. What had to be done was done. Yes, it had its flaws, and in comparison with S1, i expected so much more, but this wasn't bad either. I would give the season 6/10, finale 7/10 and show overall 8/10.
